# The Spare Key

The first thing I found in my father’s coat was a receipt for six lemons. The second was a key with a paper tag that said NOT THE SHED.

He had been dead for twelve days, and I was beginning to resent how funny he could still be.

The coat hung in the back hall, where it had hung every November through March for as long as I could remember. It was brown, with a corduroy collar and a burn on one sleeve from the year he tried to teach himself to weld. My mother had died three winters earlier. Since then he had started buying his own clothes, mostly at the farm supply store. Whenever I complimented a shirt, he would tell me how much it cost. Whenever I didn’t, he would tell me anyway.

I put the key in my pocket and took the coat out to the car. Then I brought it back inside. I had been doing a lot of that.

My brother, Nick, was coming on Saturday with his van. We had agreed that he would take the furniture and I would deal with the papers. What he meant by *the furniture* was the good table and perhaps the bed. What he meant by *the papers* was everything else in the house, declining in size until we reached, at last, the pin that held two spare buttons to a card.

At eleven someone knocked on the back door.

It was a woman in a blue raincoat, holding half a cake on a plate.

“Is this a bad time?” she asked.

I told her that it was not a particularly good one, but that I had no reason to expect improvement.

She looked at me closely. “You must be Helen.”

The woman’s name was Ruth. She lived on Daley Street and worked at the pharmacy. I knew neither of these things until she told me. She knew that I lived in Leeds, that I taught geography, that I had once backed my father’s car into a water butt, and that I had a son who had been born with six fingers on his left hand.

“Five now,” I said.

“Yes,” she said. “Your dad gave me updates.”

She put the cake on the counter. One side had been cut cleanly down the middle, and icing sagged over the exposed edge.

“I’d have brought the whole thing, but I didn’t know I was going to bring any of it until I’d started eating.”

I got out two plates.

My father, it turned out, had kept a key for Ruth. On Monday a man was coming to service her boiler, and she couldn’t find her own spare. She had let her ex-husband have it when he moved out, so he could come back for his bicycle. The bicycle was still in the kitchen, but the spare key had moved with him to Hull.

“Which is the sort of thing he’s very good at,” she said. “Moving something that isn’t the thing you asked him to move.”

I took the key out of my pocket.

“Not mine,” she said. “Mine’s got one of those rubber hats on it. Green.”

We tried the biscuit tin in the hall. My father had kept keys there since my childhood, though none of us had ever called it the key tin. Inside were two golf tees, a small plastic cow, and twenty-three keys.

Three wore green hats.

“Well,” Ruth said, “I’ve been thinking I should get to know the neighbours.”

We spread the contents of the tin over the kitchen table. Some of the keys had labels. BOAT, said one. We lived forty miles from the sea, and my father had distrusted rivers on the grounds that you could never see what they were up to. Another said MARGARET—ASK FIRST. Margaret was my mother. A third said simply OH DEAR.

Ruth held up a narrow brass key.

“That might be the church.”

“Did he go to church?”

“Not in a religious capacity.”

“What other capacity is there?”

“He lowered a carpet cleaner down the cellar stairs on a rope once.”

I waited for the rest of the story. Ruth ate another bite of cake. Apparently that was the whole thing.

She took a green key at random and went home to try it. It worked. She rang to tell me, then rang again a minute later to ask if I’d found a wooden clothes peg among the keys. There was a woman called Jean, she said, who might want one of them back.

“Why a clothes peg?”

“Your dad said she never remembered the colour of her front door. I think he was making fun of her.”

The peg was at the bottom of the tin, firmly attached to a key.

“Red door,” Ruth added. “I don’t know why she’s got such trouble with it.”

By two o’clock I had eaten another piece of cake and made a list.

1. Ruth, green.
2. Jean, peg.
3. Boat?
4. Margaret.

I had planned to spend the afternoon separating my father’s bank statements from the offers to lend him money. Instead I walked over to Jean’s. I had lived in the town until I was eighteen. I could remember where the drains flooded, which gardens had once contained dogs, and the exact location of a public telephone that had been removed in 2003. I had no idea where any of the people lived.

Jean answered her red door wearing slippers with hard soles. She took the key, examined the peg, and said, “I wondered where that went.”

She meant the peg. It was one of a set made by her grandson in a woodworking class. He had carved a J into each half. One J was backwards.

“What happened to the others?”

“Most of them broke. He was only little.”

She turned the peg over a few times and asked if I’d like a cup of tea. I said I had better keep moving. At that point I still imagined I was running an errand.

BOAT belonged to a man named Arthur, who had built a canoe in a lockup behind the carpet shop. The canoe was too wide to get out. He knew this because my father had measured it for him. He had known it, in fact, for nine years.

“You could take the doorframe off,” I said.

“Oh, we considered it.”

“Or tip the canoe on its side?”

“Yes, we considered that too. Would you like to see it?”

He meant the canoe. I went with him to the lockup. It was pale and glossy and much prettier than I had expected. Arthur couldn’t tell me what kind of wood he’d used without telling me first about the man who sold it to him, and the man who sold it to him turned out to have a daughter I’d shared a desk with in primary school. By the time we got back to Arthur’s house I had learned that the canoe would fit through the door if Arthur took off the two handles he’d fitted to carry it by. It had taken him three weekends to make the handles. He wasn’t ready.

“Your dad used to come and sit in it,” he said at the gate.

“On the ground?”

“Yes, Helen. On the ground. Where did you think he sat in it?”

I hadn’t thought my father sat in a canoe at all. The one time I’d asked him to come boating with me, on a small ornamental lake with a café in the middle, he said if I wanted him to pay nine pounds for coffee I could at least give it to him on land.

“Did he get in properly?” I asked. “Legs all the way inside?”

“Of course. We both got in. I was at the back.”

There was no way to ask what I wanted to ask without sounding like an idiot. *What did he look like in there? Was he happy? Where did he put his hands?* Arthur had already given me everything he thought there was to give.

At home I turned on the kitchen light. It was only four, but the lawn had gone the greenish grey it went before rain. I took the key marked MARGARET—ASK FIRST to the small bureau in the sitting room. My mother had answered correspondence there. She owned three fountain pens, one of which worked. When I was a child she used to give me her airmail envelopes to hold up to the light, so I could see how little paper there was between our street and Melbourne.

The key didn’t fit.

I tried the little tin box where she’d kept foreign coins, then the old writing case upstairs. I tried the cabinet in the bathroom although it had no lock. I was standing on the landing holding the key against a screw head, which is how far I’d got with things, when Nick let himself in.

“You said Saturday,” I called.

“It is Saturday.”

He came upstairs in his work boots and sat on the top step. There was a white strip of skin on his wrist where he usually wore his watch.

“I left the van running,” he said.

“Why?”

“I don’t know. I suppose I thought I’d come in and you’d be standing next to a table.”

I sat down beside him and showed him the key.

“That’s for the little padlock on the back gate,” he said.

“There isn’t a padlock on the back gate.”

“There was when he wanted to cut down her lilac.”

I remembered the lilac. I didn’t remember anyone wanting to cut it down. By the time I started coming home with a child of my own, the lilac was gone, and there was a place beside the gate where my father could stand with his arms full and push it open with his shoulder.

“She locked it so he couldn’t get the wheelbarrow through,” Nick said. “I was here that weekend. I’d come for the drill.”

“Did you get it?”

“No. I got a cup of tea from each of them in a different room.”

For a while we listened to the van running. Eventually Nick went out and turned it off. When he came back we moved the table six inches, discovered the rug underneath was a different colour where nobody had walked on it, and put the table back. Then he fetched two mugs from the cupboard, chose one without a chip for himself, reconsidered, and gave it to me.

I could tell from the size of his van that he’d hoped to bring the table home. I could also tell that he had not cleared a place for it. His wife would have asked him where it was going, and he would have said, with the unreasonable confidence he generally reserved for household acquisitions, *I’ll find somewhere.*

“Did you want the table?” I asked.

“Yes. Not today.”

I told him about Arthur’s canoe. He didn’t laugh at first.

“Dad was in it?”

“Apparently they both got in.”

“Which end was he?”

“The front.”

“Right,” Nick said. “So he had to get past Arthur to get out.”

This was the first thing anyone had said about the canoe that took proper account of our father, who couldn’t sit in the middle of a row at the cinema. Even if the room was empty he wanted the aisle. I pictured him in the lockup with his feet stretched out, not asking Arthur to move.

Nick took the cake plate over to the sink. There was a thin curl of icing left at the edge, and he scraped it up with his thumb.

“Have you tried that key in the shed?” he asked.

I showed him the tag.

“Yes,” he said, “but have you?”

We went out in the rain. The key slid into the shed lock as easily as if we’d done this every day. I turned it; the door swung in and caught on a bag of compost. Nick pushed hard enough to get his head through and found the light.

The shed had a concrete floor and smelt of cold soil. There were four screwdrivers stuck upright in a flowerpot, though I had spent nearly an hour looking for one in the house. A bicycle pump hung off a nail. Along one wall my father had put up shelves and written directly on the wood in pencil: string, washers, good jars. Beneath *good jars* there was a single jar, with a crack running from the rim nearly to the base.

Nick pulled a garden chair out from under the bench and opened it. One of the straps had been replaced with a length of old belt. He sat down and looked at his feet.

“He always made me fetch the chairs,” he said.

“He made everyone fetch the chairs.”

“No, I mean when he came round to ours. He never sat down until I’d brought another one out for him. Even if there were already chairs.”

“Were the others any good?”

“Of course they were. I’d just bought them.” Nick picked at the old belt. “They were those low ones, though.”

I sat on the bag of compost. Rain on the shed roof made the room feel smaller. At first there was the sort of quiet in which I expected Nick to start talking, and then he didn’t, and I stopped expecting it. From where I sat I could see the lower half of the garden through the open door. The big slab we’d used for hopscotch was grey except for a hand’s width under the eaves, where it was white. The rain was getting in at one corner of the roof. A single drop landed on the back of my wrist. I moved my hand.

“Who do you think he was trying to fool?” I said, holding up the tag.

“Us, probably.”

“He didn’t have anything worth stealing.”

“Maybe he just wanted us to knock.”

Nick recognised the old garage key by a nick he had filed in it himself, at fourteen, so that he could find it in his pocket without turning on a light. We established that there were five keys to the back door, one to a bicycle lock in the canal, and at least two that had belonged to cars with windows you wound down by hand.

“Your dad brought me the lemons,” she said. “I told him to get four and he brought six. He said two of them looked a bit small.”

I wanted to know whether he’d carried them over in the paper bag or tucked them into his coat. I wanted to know if the lemons had rolled about on the counter and he’d had to stop one with his hand. I could have asked Ruth and she might have remembered. But the boiler man called out to ask her a question, and while she bent to look inside the cupboard I put the jar in my bag and let myself out.

Before I left town, I went to see Arthur again. I’d been thinking about the handles.

“They don’t have to come off forever,” I said. “You can put them back on outside.”

He gave me a long look. “Yes, I understand how screws work.”

I told him I could come back the following weekend. Nick could bring the van. We might be able to take the canoe somewhere.

“Where?”

I hadn’t got that far. There was a reservoir north of town, but I didn’t know whether you could put a boat on it. There was the ornamental lake with the café, if we could stand the looks we’d get from the man who rented out the pedal boats.

“Or just outside,” I said. “We could start with outside.”

Arthur put on his shoes. We walked down to the lockup and stood there looking at the canoe. He ran his fingers over one of the handles, and I saw why it had taken him three weekends. It was wide enough to get your whole hand through, with room left over, and rounded where your palm would go. The ends fitted so closely to the side of the boat that I couldn’t tell how they’d been joined.

“Show me how you did that,” I said.

He looked about for somewhere we could sit. There was a folding stool by the door, but only one. So he held the canoe steady while I stepped in, then passed me the stool to set on the floor beside us, where he could put his tea. I sat at the front. From down there I couldn’t see the handles at all. Arthur reached over my shoulder and showed me where to put my hand.
